issue_context.title: Add virtual table for non-QFE updates (Windows only)
issue_context.body:
<!-- Thank you for contributing to osquery! -->

# Feature request

<!--
Please follow this template.
Before submitting an issue search for duplicates.
-->

### What new feature do you want?
Currently osQuery provides the `patches` table to retrieve Windows updates (https://osquery.io/schema/5.0.1#patches). However, as noted in the documentation, 

> This does not include patches applied via MSI or downloaded from Windows Update (e.g. Service Packs).

This seems to be a limitation of the underlying class that is used to generate this table (https://github.com/osquery/osquery/blob/master/osquery/tables/system/windows/patches.cpp) as `Win32_QuickFixEngineering` only returns quick fix engineering (QFE) updates.

The request here is to add a new virtual table for Windows devices which includes the patches downloaded from the Windows Update service.

<!-- Please describe with as much detail as possible. Include examples. -->

### How is this new feature useful?
There may be some compliance requirements to have visibility into all updates installed on a Windows machine. As it stands, this is not possible since you can only retrieve QFE updates. 
<!-- Describe how can this make osquery better or how you intend to use it. -->

### How can this be implemented?
You can take advantage of the `Microsoft.Update.Session` session object/the Windows Update Agent API. I found this article that has a short script showing this in action: https://social.technet.microsoft.com/wiki/contents/articles/4197.windows-how-to-list-all-of-the-windows-and-software-updates-applied-to-a-computer.aspx#Microsoft_Update_Client_Install_History

I was able to run the script in the article:
```
$Session = New-Object -ComObject "Microsoft.Update.Session"
$Searcher = $Session.CreateUpdateSearcher()

$historyCount = $Searcher.GetTotalHistoryCount()

$Searcher.QueryHistory(0, $historyCount) | Select-Object Title, Description, Date,

    @{name="Operation"; expression={switch($_.operation){

        1 {"Installation"}; 2 {"Uninstallation"}; 3 {"Other"}

}}}
```
on a Windows 10 machine and it correctly returned all the patches installed via the Windows Update.

A few caveats with this solution:
* This returns the QFE updates that are also listed in the `patches` table. These should probably be filtered out to avoid data redundancy
* The script above does not include patches installed via a MSI. I think it would make sense to have 2 separate virtual tables: one for updates installed via MSI and another for updates installed via the Windows Update service. This request is _only_ for the Windows Update service.
<!-- It's okay to leave this empty if you don't know. -->
